canberra.title: Man shot dead after allegedly pointing loaded rifle at police
canberra.snippet: A man who was shot dead after allegedly aiming a loaded rifle at the first responders who tried to help him following a car crash was kno...
canberra.content:
5 October 2026

Start the conversation

The fatal shooting happened on a country lane north of Yass. Image: Screenshot.

A man who was shot dead after allegedly aiming a loaded rifle at the first responders who tried to help him following a car crash was known to police.

An independent review will be conducted into the incident, which happened north of Yass on Sunday afternoon.

Police were called to Corringle Lane near Rugby Road, Rugby, about 84 km north of Yass, at about 2:50 pm following reports a car had been driven into a tree and into a ditch.

The Chrysler station wagon had crashed into a tree and the driver appeared to be unconscious in the front of the car. When police approached the man to help, he allegedly aimed a loaded rifle at them before being shot by police.

Police began to perform CPR but he died at the scene.

While the man has not yet been formally identified, he was known to police and they believe he was 45 years old.

NSW Police southern region commander, Assistant Commissioner Stephen Hegarty said it was too early to tell how many police discharged their firearms, but six officers were on the scene.

“As they approached that vehicle, they tried to speak and communicate with that person who did not respond,” he said.

“He then took possession of a firearm and pointed it directly at the police officer.

“At that point, I can confirm that police opened fire and he was struck with a number of rounds.

“I can confirm that that firearm was a loaded firearm.”

Assistant Commissioner Hegarty said a crime scene was established immediately and at 4 pm on Sunday he declared it a critical incident, to be investigated by State Crime Command’s Homicide Squad.

“This is a normal process,” he said.

Assistant Commissioner Hegarty offered his condolences to the man’s family and friends.

“They’ve been going through some difficult times today … my thoughts are with you,” he said.

He said his thoughts were also with the first responders at the scene, particularly the police officers.

“They turned up to a job after a call of assistance from members of the public,” he said.

“From that time they were involved in an incident that will probably stay with them and their families for the rest of their lives.”

Assistant Commissioner Hegarty praised the bravery of the officers involved.

“They were quite close to the car … they were trying to get to the person to render assistance and check on his condition,” he said.

“They were quite brave walking up to that point, so I commend them for their bravery.

“We’ve already had professional health carers speak to them [and] engage with those officers.

“My support is absolutely behind the police, and hopefully we can get through this whole incident well.”

The independent review will be conducted by the Professional Standards Command, with oversight from the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission.

Anyone with information about this incident is urged to contact Crime Stoppers: 1800 333 000. Information is managed on a confidential basis.

canberra.title: Andrew Sayers remembered posthumously in Canberra with an exhibition of his landscape paintings
canberra.snippet: For almost three decades, Andrew Sayers (1957-2015) was one of the most influential and respected figures in the Canberra visual arts sce...
canberra.content:
5 October 2026

Start the conversation

Andrew Sayers, Beach Evening, 2011, gouache on paper, 27 x 40 cm. Photo: Offmarket Gallery.

For almost three decades, Andrew Sayers (1957-2015) was one of the most influential and respected figures in the Canberra visual arts scene.

Born in England, he emigrated with his family to Australia in 1964 at age seven. In 1979, the year he completed his Fine Arts studies at the University of Sydney, the Art Gallery of New South Wales snapped him up and appointed him curatorial assistant.

In 1981, he took up the appointment as assistant director of the Newcastle Region Art Gallery for four years. In 1985, he became curator of Australian drawings at the National Gallery of Australia, a curatorial brief that quickly expanded to include watercolours and colonial paintings, and he also served as assistant director.

While still in his 20s, he had a string of important major exhibitions to his name, including the work of Albert Tucker, Sidney Nolan and James Gleeson.

Several major books followed, including Drawing in Australia (1989), Aboriginal Artists of the 19th century (1994), New Worlds from Old (1998) and Australian Art (2001).

Andrew Sayers, Rock Platform, Coledale, 2014, gouache on paper, 22 x 32 cm. Photo: Offmarket Gallery.

After leaving the National Gallery in 1998, he was appointed inaugural director of the National Portrait Gallery, which he led for a dozen years, delivering a new function-designed building, establishing the collection, and creating a string of major popular exhibitions.

The late Gordon Darling, who, together with his wife Marilyn Darling, was the gallery’s major patron, told me that without Andrew there would not have been a National Portrait Gallery.

In 2010, Sayers became director of the National Museum of Australia, but three years into a five-year contract, he quit in a shock announcement to join his wife Perry and their three daughters, who had earlier moved to Melbourne.

In May 2014, Sayers was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer and died in October of the following year. It is impossible to view this exhibition of his landscape gouaches without still feeling the pain of the recent loss of an amazing friend.

Andrew Sayers, Two volcanoes, Mt Moorookyle and Mt Kooroocheang, 2015, gouache on paper, 26 x 36 cm. Photo: Offmarket Gallery.

Sayers was a ridiculously gifted individual. He possessed a brilliant scholarly mind; he was an outstanding curator and gallery director and a gifted painter. His dedication to his day job left little time to paint en plein air, and he produced most of his paintings after retiring from his curatorial duties.

This exhibition of 20 small-scale gouache paintings on paper was executed between 2014 and 2015, with the sole exception of Beach Evening, 2011, which, with its simple abstracted colour masses, is a highlight in the show.

Sayers exhibited his paintings for the first time in September 2014, as he would jokingly say, “off Broadway”, at Mister Jones in the heart of Bermagui.

In May 2015, a second, much larger exhibition was held in Melbourne and then, posthumously, in 2015 at the Beaver Galleries in Canberra. All these exhibitions were wonderfully successful in both sales and critical acclaim.

Andrew Sayers, Rocks Awash, Coledale, 2014, gouache on paper, 22 x 32 cm. Photo: Offmarket Gallery.

The exhibition at the Barton ArtBox brings to the fore Sayers’s lightness of touch, spontaneity, a breathing atmospheric quality and his gift of saying so much with very few marks on the paper. Pieces including Rock Platform, Coledale, 2014, Rocks Awash, Coledale, 2014, Two volcanoes, Mt Moorookyle and Mt Kooroocheang, 2015, and Mt Moorookyle I, 2015, are among the show’s more successful works.

Over many years, Sayers built up a knowledge of visual literacy and now applied it with freedom and ease, so the sketches appear to breathe and float over the surface of the paper.

His favourite medium, gouache – a slightly opaque, water-based medium sometimes called poster paint in Australia – suggests form without articulating detail. A floating lightness prevails throughout the exhibition.

We are emotionally too close to the artist’s passing to be able to stand back and objectively evaluate his contribution to Australian art. However, it is amazing how much he managed to pack into his 58 years, and it remains to be seen how he will be best remembered – as a scholar, an art gallery director and curator or as an artist.

Andrew Sayers, Mt Moorookyle I, 2015, gouache on paper, 26 x 36 cm. Photo: Offmarket Gallery.

Andrew Sayers: The Capital and beyond: The landscapes of Andrew Sayers is now open at the Barton ArtBox, 7 Young Street, Barton. It closes on 31 October and is open Friday to Sunday from 11 am to 5 pm.

canberra.title: Canberra Health Services and UC expand lung rehab services
canberra.snippet: The wait time for Canberrans to access pulmonary rehabilitation services is expected to drop by up to two years as Canberra Health Servic...
canberra.content:
5 October 2026

Start the conversation

The University of Canberra will soon be providing pulmonary rehabilitation to patients in the north side of the ACT as CHS aims to more than double its services. Photo: Canberra Health Services.

The wait time for Canberrans to access pulmonary rehabilitation services is expected to drop by up to two years as Canberra Health Services and the University of Canberra expand access.

As part of Canberra Health Service’s (CHS) partnership with UC, Canberra Hospital will double its capacity, while the university will establish a northside program in the coming months.

The new northside clinic is expected to provide rehabilitation visits to 375 patients with chronic lung disease, primarily chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), each year.

These additional services are estimated to reduce hospital admissions by about 480 bed days each year, saving about $1.4 million annually.

Physiotherapy students from the University of Canberra will work at the UC Health Clinics as part of their work-integrated learning placements, under the close supervision of experienced CHS clinical staff.

Minister for Health Dr Marisa Paterson welcomed the partnership between Canberra Health Services and the University of Canberra.

“The ACT Government is committed to delivering high-quality healthcare closer to home for Canberrans. Expanding these services will enable more targeted care, improve patient outcomes, and support a more efficient and responsive public health system.

“The expansion of pulmonary rehabilitation services is a positive outcome for Canberrans living with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, who will be able to access the support they need sooner, at a convenient northside or southside location.

“This arrangement is also helping to build our allied professional workforce of the future through high-quality, supervised training for University of Canberra students in a clinical setting.”

Deputy Dean of the University of Canberra’s Faculty of Health Bernie Bissett said the partnership is the newest example of the close relationship UC has with CHS.

“The Faculty of Health at the University of Canberra is delighted to have collaborated with CHS staff to bring this project to life,” she said.

“We see the value of improving access to pulmonary rehabilitation for more people in the Canberra region, and the UC Health Clinics are the perfect home for Pulmonary Rehab for Canberra’s northsiders.

“We also know that expansion of this program helps us expertly train our future workforce of allied health professionals to deliver evidence-based and person-centred care, which is what we are all about at UC.”

Lung Foundation Australia’s clinical programs, research and innovation general manager Alicia Goodwin said the expansion responds to a clear and longstanding need for greater access to vital pulmonary services across the ACT.

“Pulmonary rehabilitation is one of the most effective non-pharmacological interventions available for people living with chronic lung disease,” she said.

“It helps people manage their symptoms, remain active and independent, improve their quality of life and reduce their risk of hospitalisation.

“We commend the ACT Government and Canberra Health Services for prioritising respiratory care and look forward to continuing to work together to improve lung health outcomes for people across the ACT.”
