canberra.title: Beyond Pad Thai: Akaluck opens the door to regional Thai dishes
canberra.snippet: One of my favourite things about visiting restaurants is learning more about regional cuisines and the many different cooking styles that...
canberra.content:
The duck nam tok was delicious. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

One of my favourite things about visiting restaurants is learning more about regional cuisines and the many different cooking styles that make up a national food identity. Thai food is generally well loved in Australia – who doesn’t love a Massaman Curry or Pad Thai? But this diverse cuisine offers much more.

Akaluck Gungahlin, on the edge of Yerrabi Pond, has a wide-ranging menu that covers your go-to Thai favourites and showcases regional Isan cuisine from northeastern Thailand. There’s a full page of menu items showcasing the spicy flavours of Isan food, so of course we had to try something. The Akaluck specialties pages also had us hooked, so we were in for a night of Thai food that went well beyond Pad Thai!

We decided on the spicy crispy rice (an Isan dish), roasted duck Nam Tok and the Akaluck eggplant. The chef sent out two little bites of pork floss and sweet chilli jam on crackers, and a plate of prawn crackers while we waited: a lovely and tasty gesture of generosity!

Crispy fried eggplant in Akaluck’s special sauce should be on every table. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

The duck Nam Tok came with a side of lettuce, tomato and cucumber slices, and the succulent slices of duck were mixed with plenty of fresh herbs and raw onion. The zingy lemon dressing cut through the fatty duck, and a sprinkle of roasted, ground rice added textural crunch and a toasty taste. The whole flavour profile reminded me of larb, but with sliced meat instead of minced. The Isan region shares a border and many culinary connections with Laos, so it makes sense that there are plenty of similarities.

The crispy rice was a revelation; I’ve never had anything quite like it.

Crispy rice is beloved around the world in various forms: the tahdig crust of rice in Iran comes to mind. This dish takes a crispy layer of rice, breaks it up and combines it with coriander, mint, shallots, ginger, peanuts and roasted, shredded coconut.

I can imagine it began life as a way to zhuzh up leftover rice into a more exciting meal! We opted to include the fermented pork sausage in the dish as well, which added salty, umami notes throughout.

Each bite had a brilliantly varied texture, and the herbs and ginger added freshness and flavour. Totally yum.

The spicy crispy rice was a standout dish. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

The crispy rice and duck dish both came with a double chilli heat warning, but most of the heat came from the whole, dried red chillies scattered throughout the dish, which you could easily pick out for a more manageable burn.

The fried eggplant was another winner. The battered pieces of eggplant had a crispy exterior which gradually succumbed to the sticky sauce. Inside, the eggplant flesh was creamy. Tossed through with other veggies, this was a thoroughly delightful vegetarian dish which I’d happily order again.

The restaurant was quiet late on a Tuesday evening, but I overheard the chef and manager chatting about the next day’s bookings, so it sounds like it gets busier later in the week.

They also offer a breakfast menu which I’d love to try – the rice porridge and spicy scrambled eggs sound delicious!

Akaluck Restaurant is located at 76 Phillis Ashton Circuit, Gungahlin. They are open from 8.30 am to 9 pm on weekends, and from 5 to 9 pm Tuesday to Friday. Follow Akaluck on Facebook.

canberra.title: After losing three generations to breast cancer, Lauren encourages everyone to ‘get comfortable with breast health’
canberra.snippet: Head to the pub on a Sunday afternoon and you don’t expect to find people standing around naked. But that’s exactly what’s planned for 18...
canberra.content:
Lauren Sutherland says breast health shouldn’t be taboo – it should be routine. Photo: Nathan Harradine-Hale.

Head to the pub on a Sunday afternoon and you don’t expect to find people standing around naked.

But that’s exactly what’s planned for 18 October at PJs in the City.

Bare it for Breast Cancer will feature three live drawing models posing for artists of any skill level, while BreastScreen ACT will answer “all of your boob and mammogram-related questions”.

The event aims to bring together lessons on art, body confidence and women’s health, with half of all ticket sales donated to BreastScreen ACT.

It’s another bold initiative for Lauren Sutherland, founder of Tipsy Sketching Club, which runs life modelling workshops and drawing events in pubs and clubs across Canberra, NSW and Victoria.

While Lauren herself hasn’t always been comfortable with her body, she’s never been afraid of a challenge.

It was her personal quest towards body confidence that first led her to step out of her comfort zone – and clothes – to pose nude for a group of strangers.

“There’s something really special about seeing art made of yourself,” she said.

“For me, it’s created a big mindset change. The more art I see of myself, the more amazed and thankful I am for my body, however it is that day.”

Lauren hopes the empowerment and confidence women often find in life drawing will also benefit their breast health. Photo: Michael Billing.

Last year, Lauren used one such event to raise awareness and funds for breast cancer, attracting 80 attendees and raising over $1000 for the cause.

“This year we’ve set our sights on BreastScreen ACT as our charity partner, which is the region’s primary provider of free mammograms to people over 40 and greatly assists in the early detection and improved treatment outcomes for those with breast cancer.”

It’s a deeply personal cause to Lauren, whose family history has left her “very breast-aware”.

Lauren has lost three generations of women in her family to breast cancer – her mother, grandmother and great-grandmother.

Her mother, Sandra, was diagnosed at 52 when she found a suspicious lump.

After a mammogram confirmed cancer, she went on to have a lumpectomy, chemotherapy and radiation. Sandra lost her battle eight years later.

“She was an incredible artist, having studied visual arts, calligraphy and signwriting over her lifetime, and would absolutely have loved attending a life drawing event – even more so if it was in aid of breast cancer organisations.

“One of my greatest regrets is that I didn’t tap into this side of me before my Mum passed away.

“I think she’d be proud of what I’ve achieved, creating something truly my own in an industry I had no idea I’d be involved in but now couldn’t live without.”

Lauren and her Mum, Sandra Daly. Photo: Supplied

After discovering a lump aged 52, Sandra battled with breast cancer for eight years. Photo: Supplied

Lauren’s Grandmother’s cancer journey was shorter, as she pursued natural and alternative medicines, which Lauren said “didn’t have great effect.”

Lauren has undergone gene testing, annual breast MRIs and plans to celebrate her 40th birthday with a mammogram. And she never misses her monthly self-check.

“Feel it on the first!” she said.

“The earlier you catch something, the better the treatment outcome will be, and that’s what BreastScreen ACT can support us with.”

Lauren believes being comfortable with your body is an important first step to being aware of any changes.

“I hope people continue learning about their own bodies – whether it be by monthly self-checks or just finding something that looks or feels different.

“Breast health doesn’t have to be taboo – the more open we are about it, the more comfortable people will be to seek screening and treatment.”

Bare It for Breast Cancer will take place at PJs in the City on Sunday 18 October. Book tickets at Tipsy Sketching.

australia.title: Peter and Maria were mourned by people who loved them. So how did they end up in unmarked communal graves?
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Authorities are failing to notify family, friends and outreach workers before burying strangers in shared plots, a Guardian Au...
australia.content:
The track marks have dried in the mud beside Peter Giesel’s unmarked grave. The digger is long gone, although other signs of work remain.

A disused shovel. A traffic cone. A stretch of earth where the soil is yet to settle, sandwiched between an old set of headstones and a dirt walkway at Sydney’s Rookwood general cemetery.

Nothing tells you Giesel is here – no headstone, cross or plaque.

There’s no sign that the New South Wales government buried him in this grave with three others on a single day in late June, four strangers united only by the plot they share.

Giesel’s sister, Nicole, is confused and devastated after belatedly learning that her older brother had been put in an unmarked communal grave.

So is his close friend Elaine Grady, who would spend hours each day on the phone to Peter from the US, joking and laughing, sharing pictures of American cars, and dreaming up plans for the out-of-work mechanic to escape his difficult life in Australia.

“How could such a heartless thing happen to someone who gave so much of his heart to others?” she says.

Giesel’s plot sits in a row of nine unmarked graves dug in the first half of this year to hold people the NSW government has designated “persons without means” – those unable to afford their own funerals.

The designation gives the state control over the handling of their remains, leading to about 98 burials, 293 cremations and 22 ash interments each year.

A Guardian Australia investigation has found that the process is sending hundreds of poor and vulnerable Australians into unmarked communal graves like Giesel’s, which typically hold four to six people each.

The three-month investigation, encompassing evidence from family, friends and support workers alongside analysis of cemetery records and aerial and satellite imagery, has also identified serious failures that are putting people into unmarked graves unnecessarily.

In six cases uncovered by the Guardian, friends, community leaders and family were either not told of the use of unmarked communal graves or not given a proper chance to intervene and pay or crowdfund for a proper burial or marker, a likely breach of government policy.

Guardian Australia has also discovered that at least 18 individuals known to Sydney homelessness services have been placed in the unmarked graves since 2016.

In one case, the rough sleeper Roger Davies was put in a grave with four strangers without his sister’s knowledge because police lacked her current contact details.

His sister, Chantel Dubsky, was alive and well in Adelaide, and would have paid for her brother’s cremation and repatriation.

She describes the failing as “unspeakable”.

Prominent leaders in Sydney’s homelessness sector are outraged by the revelations, saying they were not informed about the use of unmarked communal graves and were never given the chance to intervene and pay for proper burials for clients or former clients.

“Some people in the homelessness sector are aware that destitute funerals exist, and some may have attended them in the past as case workers, often as the only person present, myself included,” says Jon Swain, the Australian Alliance to End Homelessness NSW homelessness adviser.

“What we were not aware of, and what has caused considerable alarm, is that people were potentially being buried in unmarked communal graves with multiple individuals in the same plot.”

Guardian Australia has also identified two Vietnam war veterans buried in unmarked communal graves in 2024 and 2025. Both served in the Royal Australian Navy.

The federal government runs a funding assistance program designed to pay for the funerals of indigent veterans. The Department of Veterans’ Affairs confirmed it “has not been approached to help fund the burials of destitute persons since 2020”.

Queensland is also using unmarked graves for burials, though it does not use communal interments in the same manner as NSW.

The situation in both states contrasts sharply with that in Victoria, where the state trustee uses a rural cemetery at Ballan to bury its most disadvantaged citizens in single plots, each with a marking.

It does this as a “matter of respect for the deceased” and to ensure families and friends have a place to visit.

The process costs $3,000 a burial, a fixed rate that, if adopted in NSW, would cost the state government at most about $360,000 a year.

“We just feel like this is the appropriate way of honouring the deceased, to put them in their individual graves and to mark it,” says the State Trustees Victoria chief executive, Melissa Reynolds.

“I don’t think there’s any right or wrong in the way that different states take a position on these things.

“We just think … it’s important should anybody come forward at a future point, to recognise that they have got their own site and have been treated with dignity at the end of their life.”

The revelations have prompted an immediate response.

NSW Health delivered an apology to the dead and their loved ones, acknowledging they had not always been treated with the dignity and respect they deserved.

The health minister, Ryan Park, has also intervened, describing the past failings as “unacceptable”.

The NSW government says it hopes recent changes may improve the process and has flagged further reforms, including working with charities and non-government organisations to find funding for funerals.

‘Buddy was his lifeline’

There’s a photo of Peter Giesel that Grady loves to share.

He is looking down at the camera, a weary smile on his face. On his lap sits Buddy, a brown and white border collie.

Buddy was Giesel’s whole world, a source of unconditional love in an isolated and difficult life.

“Buddy was his lifeline, the reason he got up every morning, his partner and his best friend,” Grady says.

Giesel had a difficult upbringing.

His brother died of a brain tumour when he was in primary school. Nicole remembers spending long stretches with her brother at the Ronald McDonald House in Camperdown while their parents spoke to doctors and surgeons.

She has fond memories of a nurse taking the siblings to the movies, and of wandering the grounds of Camperdown children’s hospital, finding trees to climb.

The family struggled for money in later years.

As an adult, Giesel lived with his father in a public housing property and Grady remembers ordering groceries online from her home in Rhode Island and having them delivered to them, worried that they weren’t eating.

The pair met on Facebook about 10 years ago. They quickly struck up a close friendship.

Giesel reconditioned old engines and Grady delivered auto parts across Rhode Island and neighbouring states for a living. He loved all things American cars.

“My daily journey for work was like attending a car show, so I would bring him along with me for the ride,” Grady says.

Giesel came to know Grady’s family. He’d play them Australian music – Cold Chisel were a favourite – and Grady watched as her friend tried, with limited success, to learn guitar.

“He would play songs for me and it would make me smile,” she says. “I always told him it was great while I secretly turned the volume down. I’m pretty sure he knew but neither of us ever said anything.”

Then Grady watched on, feeling helpless, as her friend suffered hit after hit in his final year.

When his father died in September 2023, Giesel was booted from the home they shared, losing many of his possessions. He ended up in a caravan outside his sister’s place in Minto, south-western Sydney.

“All he had left was his dog, Buddy, and what he could carry out with him,” Grady says.

Two months later, Buddy was hit by a car. Giesel had to put him down, a decision that broke him.

He sank into depression.

“Peter was never the same,” Grady says. “He became quiet and kept to himself most of the time, sometimes going days without contacting me, despite my best efforts to reach him.”

About 10pm on 14 August 2024, police were called for a welfare check on Giesel. They found him inside the caravan, dead, from what the coroner says were natural causes.

Nicole says she had no money to pay for her brother’s funeral. But she also says she was never told that an unmarked or communal grave would be used for his remains.

“This is the first I’ve heard of this and I’m devastated,” she says. “I feel sick.”

The policy is clear. NSW health authorities are supposed to do everything they can to identify people willing to pay for a funeral.

That includes contacting “friends or other interested parties associated with the deceased to pay for a burial or cremation”.

And NSW Health is supposed to consider using “publicly available funding avenues (such as crowdfunding)”.

Policy documents state that this is designed to “help to avoid causing unnecessary distress to people who may have wished to make other funeral arrangements and been willing to pay the funeral costs”.

Grady was not hard to find. She had posted on Giesel’s publicly accessible Facebook profile, informing others of his death and paying tribute to her late friend two years before he was eventually buried.

Had she been contacted, she says, she would have helped to pay for the funeral. Giesel’s other friends in the US would have contributed, she adds, had she set up a GoFundMe page.

“This news was devastating, not only to me, but to my family who loved him just as much as I did,” she says. “If nothing else, you would think he deserved to be buried in his own space, with a marker saying he was there.”

‘Mary fell through the cracks’

Maria Kikkert often came to work bearing gifts.

Most days she’d stop off at a small Vietnamese bakery on her way to Sydney’s north shore from her own home in Chester Hill, near Bankstown in western Sydney.

She’d turn up on the doorstep of her employers, the Cowley family from Lindfield, with fresh bánh mì rolls.

Kikkert was the Cowleys’ housekeeper for almost 20 years. Kathy Cowley says she was there so long she became part of the family.

The rolls were just the start.

Kikkert brought clothes for Kathy’s daughter, a coffee machine for their kitchen and a pie-maker for Kathy.

“She was such a wonderful help, such a kind, generous person,” Cowley says. “So generous – and yet we didn’t realise until we went to her memorial service and visited her home afterwards that she had been living in complete poverty.”

Kikkert hadn’t told the Cowleys much about her personal life.

She had a life of trauma and loss, mental ill health and poker machine addiction that had driven her to financial despair.

Kikkert’s life began to spiral out of control after her husband, Egbert, died in 2011. She began spending long stretches at the Bankstown sport club, often staying until closing time, feeding what little money she had into the machines.

She was left with no money to look after herself, one neighbour and friend said. Her home became filled with junk and she borrowed money and pawned jewellery to survive.

Her appearance became increasingly dishevelled and her neighbour grew concerned that the deterioration in her mental health was not being picked up by her doctors.

In August 2022 she was found dead at home.

“Mary fell through the cracks in the system,” the friend says, adding: “She is a victim. She’s a victim of the system, and that’s why she’s died with no money and ended up in a pauper’s grave.”

Kikkert, a Catholic, was buried as a “person without means” by the NSW government on 23 November 2022.

She was put in an unmarked grave with the remains of four others.

Cowley remembers turning up for the burial and being shocked by what she saw.

Her friend’s simple timber casket had been taken to a strange part of the cemetery, between a dirt walkway and a set of old headstones.

“I wouldn’t even know how to find it again,” she says. “It was just a patch of dirt. Several graves had been dug and some were freshly sort of covered over.

“It was Mary’s that was the only one that was open, ready for the casket, and then, following the short dedication and prayers from Mary’s parish priest, there were a couple of men just standing by, ready to fill the grave after we departed.”

Cowley says she wasn’t given a chance to provide money for the funeral, a responsibility that falls to the NSW government. The funeral director was helpful and supportive, she says, and allowed her to pay for flowers for Kikkert’s casket.

But she says she would have paid for a headstone or “something to commemorate Mary and her life”, particularly if she’d known her friend was going into an unmarked communal grave.

“I would have said that’s unacceptable if I had been asked, and I would have said, ‘Look, what can I do? How can I contribute?’”

Kikkert’s stepdaughter remembers getting a phone call the day before the burial.

It was from a funeral director, not anyone within the NSW government.

She says she was never told what the burial would entail.

“I was informed that she was having a destitute burial,” she says. “But the sentence should have gone on and said she will be with four or five other people, and there will be no marking.

“Mary had a dreadful life, and she had a dreadful time after my father died. And now she’s had a dreadful time after her death.”

The stepdaughter was using the surname “Kikkert” at the time of her stepmother’s death. She says it would have been easy for the NSW authorities to find her.

“I don’t think I’m hard to find,” she says. “As you say, you found me.”

New South Wales Health, which assumed greater control of the process from police in 2025, issued a statement apologising for past failings.

“Families and friends who have lost a loved one face many challenges managing arrangements during a time of grief, and all deceased persons should be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their financial circumstances,” a spokesperson said.

“It is clear this has not always occurred with respect to the burials or cremations for deceased people without the financial means to pay for a funeral, and NSW Health apologises for the distress this has caused to those who have lost someone they love.”

NSW Health said it had made changes to the process in 2025 and in recent months to improve the way the funerals were handled. That includes putting NSW Health Pathology in charge of deaths that occur outside of hospitals or in cases that are before the coroner.

NSW Health Pathology has created a dedicated funeral support assessment team with 6.2 full-time equivalent positions, which is focused on identifying opportunities for “alternative funeral arrangements and alternate sources of support for families and friends that may be willing to assist”.

It is also exploring further changes to improve its coordination with charities, community and religious groups and other government organisations.

Two NSW ministers, Park and the homelessness minister, Rose Jackson, said the dead and their families should be treated with respect, regardless of their financial circumstances.

“Previous arrangements have meant that this has not always been the case, and that is unacceptable,” Park said.

“Since early 2025, NSW Health has made significant changes to establish a more comprehensive and person-centred approach to ensure all deceased persons are treated with the respect and compassion they deserve.”

A spokesperson for Metropolitan Memorial Parks, which operates Rookwood general cemetery, said the NSW government did not fund it to provide grave markings for people without means.

MMP said destitute burials were not the only burial type that used multiple interments in a single plot.

The details of all those buried in Rookwood, including through the persons without means process, are published online, including the grave location, and MMP rejected any suggestion that those buried through the process were being placed between individual headstones, under walkways or in trenches.

MMP said it had identified no legislation or regulation that had given effect to the government’s 2013 promise to mark graves.

“The government covers only the cost of a basic, dignified burial or cremation,” the spokesperson said. “Permanent memorialisation, such as a bronze or stone plaque, is optional and is not funded by the state.”

‘Begging for answers I may never find’

Families and friends of others interred in the graves are now desperate for answers.

Grady has spent the past month trying to get an explanation from NSW Health and Rookwood about Giesel’s burial.

She has been stonewalled at every turn.

Her emails to NSW Health have gone unanswered. She has been told by Rookwood that the cemetery cannot answer her questions until she signs a statutory declaration stipulating why she wants the information and how she will use it.

The cemetery’s operator said in a separate statement to the Guardian that Grady was welcome to apply for a grave maker but it would need to see evidence of her identity and of her relationship to Giesel.

The only questions Grady has asked are why her friend appears to be in a grave with others and whether she can pay for a marker to be left at the plot.

“Unfortunately, there are no answers, there is no one to turn to for help, and I am left with my hands tied, begging for answers I may never find,” she says.

“Every day I miss my friend and all the craziness that came along with him. Too often I will hear a song, or scroll past a photo, and remember how much he meant to me – how many smiles and laughs we shared.

“Someday we will meet again, and go right back to the way we were. Until then, we will keep [him] alive in our memories.”

australia.title: Hundreds of Australians, including war veterans, are being buried in unmarked communal graves
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Guardian Australia investigation reveals state governments use shared graves to bury those deemed too poor to pay for funerals...
australia.content:
Vietnam veterans, rough sleepers and other impoverished Australians are being buried in unmarked communal graves often holding four or more people, a practice relatives have described as “unspeakable” and “a disgrace”.

A Guardian Australia investigation has identified more than 100 unmarked graves across New South Wales, and some in Queensland, that are being used by state governments to bury those deemed too poor to afford their own funerals.

Using evidence from family, friends and the homelessness sector, together with analysis of cemetery registries and aerial imagery, the Guardian has established that the NSW government is using bare stretches of earth between dirt walkways and old headstones at Rookwood cemetery in Sydney to bury the remains of four to six strangers together in communal graves.

Among those being buried together are war veterans, cancer sufferers, people with gambling addictions and severe mental illness, and migrants from developing countries whose families cannot afford exorbitant repatriation costs.

In at least six cases, the Guardian has identified failures by authorities that meant friends, family or support workers were either not contacted or not told of the use of unmarked and common graves. The failures are likely breaches of a NSW policy designed to “avoid causing unnecessary distress to people who may have wished to make other funeral arrangements”.

Shocked family and friends say they have been left feeling robbed.

“It’s unspeakable,” said Chantel Dubsky, whose brother Roger Davies, a rough sleeper, was buried in an unmarked grave with four strangers at Rookwood without her knowledge. “He should have had the opportunity to be laid to rest with his mother, his grandparents and the people he loved, at his home in Adelaide.

“He wasn’t just someone off the street – he was someone’s son, he was someone’s brother. He was my brother.”

By crosschecking names with homelessness services in Sydney, Guardian Australia has also identified a further 18 individuals in the communal graves who had experienced homelessness.

The homelessness sector is outraged by the revelations.

Two leaders in Sydney’s homelessness sector say they were never made aware of the practice of using unmarked communal graves and are not being given the chance to intervene on behalf of their clients to fund a proper burial.

A third service, the Rev Bill Crews Foundation, an inner-city Sydney homelessness charity, says it has repeatedly raised concerns with the state government about the possible use of unmarked and communal graves but has been ignored.

The Rev Bill Crews, who runs the foundation, identified three of his clients as being among those in the communal graves but said he had not been told about their deaths and impending burials.

“It’s outrageous,” Crews said. “We did not know – they would all have had a dignified funeral and a proper cremation, and their ashes would have been scattered in the sea.

The foundation regularly uses its own funds to conduct funeral services for rough sleepers when it becomes aware they have died. It was given no notification in the three cases.

“For us, it’s frustrating. Incredibly frustrating.”

Guardian Australia has also established that two veterans of the Vietnam war, who both served in the Royal Australian Navy, were buried in unmarked communal graves in 2024 and 2025.

The pair were buried despite the availability of a federal funding program run by the Department of Veterans’ Affairs to help pay for the funerals of impoverished veterans. NSW policy recommends state health authorities approach DVA in such cases.

DVA was never asked for funding for the 2024 and 2025 burials. A spokesperson said it has “not been approached to help fund the burials of destitute persons since 2020”.

The Guardian’s investigation has prompted an apology from NSW Health, which has flagged changes to improve the process, and criticism from the health minister, Ryan Park, who described the failings as “unacceptable”.

In the first half of this year alone, a 17-metre stretch of earth adjacent to a dirt pathway at Rookwood has been dug up and used to bury the remains of more than 40 people in unmarked communal graves, including a rough sleeper who was well-known to most major homelessness services.

Nothing has been left to mark the 17-metre stretch of graves. Inspections of the sites of hundreds of other burials at Rookwood since 2010 show only about a dozen are marked by crosses or plaques.

The vast majority have no crosses, plaques or headstones to name the groups of deceased in each plot. There are also no signs to indicate the presence of graves.

Older sites, where the earth has settled, appear simply as long stretches of grass.

Markings are generally not used in Queensland for the smaller number of people buried under its scheme. The use of communal graves is much rarer in that state.

The situation contrasts sharply with the process embraced by Victoria, where each individual is given their own grave and a simple marking, identifying who is interred below.

The NSW government has previously pledged to stop the use of unmarked graves for destitute burials.

That came after lobbying by Barbara Davis, who was never told that her foster daughter Christine Halpin had been buried in Rookwood in 1989.

Davis and Christine’s biological daughter Jayne say they were told by the NSW government in 2013 that the use of unmarked graves would cease. The cemetery erected a “path of remembrance” that allows people to pay more than $800 to put a plaque on a rock, about 1km from some of the gravesites, but this has been used in a few dozen cases since 2020.

Christine’s gravesite remains unmarked. Davis and Jayne are both furious.

“It is a disgrace,” Davis said. “Whether you’re a prince or a pauper, you deserve a decent burial site, even just with a wooden cross with your name on it.”

In another case, a young Fijian who came to Australia to play rugby in Leeton, in NSW’s Riverina region, was buried in a communal unmarked grave after dying of cancer in 2022.

A former Leeton mayor, Paul Maytom, now president of the Leeton Multicultural Support Group, said he had previously helped raise funds from local Solomon Islander and Vietnamese communities to provide repatriation or proper burials.

He was not informed about the Fijian’s death.

“There should be a point of contact when this type of thing happens,” Maytom said. “And you should never have a situation where someone ends up in an unmarked grave, particularly when there are community members who are willing to help pay.”

A NSW Health Pathology spokesperson apologised for the failings, acknowledging they meant the dead and families and friends were not always treated with dignity and respect.

“Families and friends who have lost a loved one face many challenges managing arrangements during a time of grief, and all deceased persons should be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their financial circumstances,” a spokesperson said.

“It is clear this has not always occurred with respect to the burials or cremations for deceased people without the financial means to pay for a funeral, and NSW Health apologises for the distress this has caused to those who have lost someone they love.”

NSW Health said it had made changes to the process in 2025 and in recent months to improve the way the funerals were handled. That includes giving NSW Health greater control, in place of police, and creating a dedicated six-person team within NSW Health Pathology to provide “alternative funeral arrangements and alternate sources of support for families and friends that may be willing to assist”.

It also flagged improving its relationships with “religious, cultural, charitable, community, and government organisations” to find funding for funerals after deaths.

Two NSW ministers, Park and the homelessness minister, Rose Jackson, said the dead and their families should be treated with respect, regardless of their financial circumstances.

“Previous arrangements have meant that this has not always been the case, and that is unacceptable,” Park said.

“Since early 2025, NSW Health has made significant changes to establish a more comprehensive and person-centred approach to ensure all deceased persons are treated with the respect and compassion they deserve.”

A spokesperson for Metropolitan Memorial Parks, which operates Rookwood general cemetery, said the NSW government did not fund it to provide grave markings for persons without means.

MMP said destitute burials were not the only burial type that used multiple interments in a single plot, and rejected any suggestion that those buried through the process were being placed between individual headstones, under walkways or in trenches.

It also said it had identified no legislation or regulation that had given effect to the government’s 2013 promise to mark graves.

australia.title: OpenAI must explain action taken to stop AI hacking Australians’ private data, chair of federal inquiry says
australia.snippet: Unions, employer groups, banks and industry experts will appear at the four-day hearings along with OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Goog...
australia.content:
OpenAI must explain how they will stop their models from inappropriately accessing Australian data, the Labor chair of the parliament’s committee on artificial intelligence has warned, ahead of federal inquiry hearings which will grill the tech company alongside Anthropic, Microsoft and Google.

Independent senator David Pocock is also demanding answers, saying OpenAI “still have a lot they need to answer” about their AI agent accessing Services Australia data on Medicare and the company’s “appalling” tardiness in notifying the federal government about the incident.

The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence will hold four days of hearings this week, hearing from tech companies as well as unions, employer groups, banks and industry experts. Tuesday’s hearing will include representatives from copyright and artists’ groups, to probe issues around access to data to train AI models, as well as the Australian Broadcasting Corportation, which warned in its submission of a “cannibalisation” of journalism and demanded AI companies be subject to the same copyright, defamation and privacy rules as news outlets.

  • Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, will front the hearing alongside Adam Cohen, the company’s head of economic policy, and Asia-Pacific national security lead, Peter Anstee. OpenAI last week apologised for the Services Australia incident and the manner in which it informed the government, saying it was “working to do better”.

But the Labor MP chairing the committee, Jo Briskey, said the company still had questions to answer.

“We have heard what happened, we understand what has occurred, and there’s some pretty problematic issues around not only the fact that these AI agents did access non-public data, but the reality was also that they took far too long to to notify us,” she said.

“We’ve seen OpenAI make its public apology to Australians. That’s important … my focus is on what do they do next? How do they assure Australians that they that this won’t happen again? And that’s a difficult question.”

Briskey said her starting point would be to interrogate how to balance the potential risks and rewards of AI, such as economic benefits as well as cyber security and defence applications. She said she would also raise concerns about online safety, scams, and how any benefits would be spread among all Australians.

“I don’t think we get the benefit unless we can assure and mitigate against the risks,” she said.

Pocock, who is also on the committee, also plans to seek more answers from OpenAI about the Services Australia incident.

“You’ve got a bunch of companies that are essentially self-regulating with Donald Trump. I don’t think many people would trust Sam Altman and OpenAI … This is supposedly a company the Australian government wants to welcome with open arms and do deals with,” he said.

“The Medicare hack stuff will be pretty well looked at through the committee process. It’s been a fairly appalling response from them.”

Altman, in an interview with Politico published on Monday, said OpenAI “believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.”

Pocock has raised alarm about the potential impacts on artists, creatives and copyrighted material and said he was still to be convinced about the technology.

“There’s still big questions over the long-term benefit of all this for Australia … Nobody has been able to answer that,” he said.

“[The government] is chasing this GDP sugar hit, but we haven’t hit the big part of the datacentre buildout yet, and we’re already [seeing] inflation going up. They want to raise GDP, but after the buildout phase, how do we get a return? Looking at how much tax big tech companies pay, it’s not much, and I don’t see how it’ll change.”

Pocock is keen to interrogate the government plans to address copyright issues. Anthropic, in its submission, suggested a form of “opt-out” model where rightsholders could request their data not be scraped; an idea SBS, in its submission, claimed was “routinely ignored or bypassed”.

Pocock said it was “hard to cop this industry saying it’s too hard to deal with rightsholders when they’re heading for multi-trillion-dollar valuations”, and said the government should “force them [AI companies] to negotiate deals.”

australia.title: Australian leaders condemn pro-Palestine vigils planned for 7 October anniversary amid Jewish commemorations
australia.snippet: Peak Jewish bodies organise ceremonies on third anniversary of attacks that triggered conflict in which 74,000 Palestinians have been kil...
australia.content:
Jewish Australians will mark the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks on Wednesday as Labor state governments condemn pro-Palestinian vigils to be held the same day.

Peak Jewish bodies have organised commemorations across the capital cities but avoided publicising locations as community members report ongoing fears for their safety since the Bondi terror attack in December.

Hamas militants killed about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took 251 others hostage in the surprise attack on Israel in 2023, triggering the ongoing Israel-Gaza war in which 74,000 Palestinians have been killed.

On the night before the anniversary, people at a Melbourne event were expected to hear a first-hand account from an Israeli soldier who was in the country during the attacks. Zionism Victoria has planned an outdoor evening ceremony on Wednesday.

Sydney’s eastern suburbs will host a dawn commemoration starting at 6.29am, to mark the time at which Hamas’ attack began and an evening community event run by the Zionist Council of NSW and backed by the United Israel Appeal, the local arm of Keren Hayesod.

“United in remembrance and resilience, we stand with Israel and the Jewish people, joined by our fellow Australians against hatred and extremism,” the evening event’s description reads.

A documentary exploring experiences of Israeli trauma professionals, After Never Again, will be screened in Canberra and Perth. The film has been produced by Kehilot to Australia or K2A, a group set up to bring Israeli youth to Australia for relief from the stress of living near active conflict.

All details, including registration, have been kept private for events planned in Brisbane and Adelaide. JWire has reported the Zionist Council of Queensland has organised a gathering open to Nepalese, Filipino and Iranian communities.

Pro-Palestine groups have also planned to mark the day, with a gathering planned at Sydney’s town hall on Wednesday evening. An organising group, Jews Against The Occupation ‘48, said their event would not be a protest but a vigil to mark Israel’s retaliatory airstrikes on Gaza on 7 October 2023, in a post on social media.

Wollongong Friends of Palestine, south of Sydney, has planned its own vigil.

A Melbourne “sit-in vigil” is planned from 10am to 5pm outside the state library of Victoria. The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has said police would act to “protect the public” if the event breached the state’s anti-vilification laws.

The New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, has said the planned vigils on the anniversary of a “horrible and violent” event were “obscene”, speaking to reporters last Wednesday.

“To choose that day, I think it’s designed to antagonise large sections of our community,” Minns said. “I’m obviously distressed on their behalf.”

Minns said supreme court and high court decisions on political communication prevented him from shutting down the Wednesday gatherings.

“They’re very difficult … for us to shut down static protests, particularly ones, as I think they’re describing it as a vigil, a silent vigil. We’ll see if it is a silent vigil.”

Further pro-Palestine rallies to mark the anniversary are planned in more than a dozen Australian cities on Sunday as part of a “global day of action” led by activist groups overseas. A Friday rally is also scheduled outside the electorate office of Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles.

australia.title: Greens pitch Zohran Mamdani-style $25.1bn plan to nationalise 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarkets
australia.snippet: Former MP and Greens Institute head, Max Chandler-Mather, says proposal for publicly owned supermarket chain will ease grocery prices Get...
australia.content:
More than 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarkets would be nationalised, and hundreds of government grocery stores opened, under a $25bn plan being put forward by former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather.

Channelling New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s plan for publicly owned grocery stores, Chandler-Mather, the boss of the party’s thinktank, the Greens Institute, wants to use new forced divestiture laws to take over major supermarket sites and three distribution centres.

The government would fund another 424 new supermarkets and 10 distribution centres, taking about 20% of the market share of commercial operators for the new non-profit network.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Chandler-Mather says the new stores – dubbed Fair Go Grocers – would save consumers as much as 22% on the average shop, or $60 per week for a four-person household. Heavy discounts would be put in place for essentials including fruit and vegetables, bread, milk and meat.

A statutory authority would be established to set prices each month, as well as minimum wholesale rates for suppliers. Its members would include experts in supermarket operations, nutrition and food science, and farming.

The federal government would pay for capital costs including land, construction, and acquisition, and stores would be located in areas of the highest need.

After an initial $25.1bn price tag over five years, Chandler-Mather says the stores would be self-funded and not require additional taxpayer cash.

By comparison, the federal government currently spends about $24bn each year on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.

“Kids are going to school hungry, families are skipping meals, people are cutting back on essentials, all because Labor has allowed Coles and Woolworths to jack up prices for extra profit, regardless of the human consequences,” Chandler-Mather said.

“Just like healthcare and education, food is essential to life. And just like Medicare and public schools, it’s time we had a public option for food.”

The proposal is similar to Mamdani’s plan for five city-owned and subsidised grocery stores, one in each of New York City’s boroughs, opening by 2029. Last month a local business group sued the Democratic Socialist mayor, arguing existing small grocery stores would be unable to compete.

The New Zealand Greens have a plan to nationalise 120 supermarkets and establish a new publicly owned chain called KiwiMark.

The Greens Institute commissioned pollsters YouGov to test public support for the proposal last month, with background on Mamdani’s plan for government-owned stores that cut out profits made by private corporations.

Voters were asked: Would you support or oppose publicly owned supermarkets being tried in Australia? A total of 84% said they strongly supported or somewhat supported the idea, while 16% somewhat or strongly opposed the idea.

Support was strongest among voters aged 25-34 (88%), among Greens voters (96%) and women (88%).

Newly elected Greens leader David Shoebridge, under pressure to spur enthusiasm and attention for the party, has welcomed the proposal, saying the Greens should be focused on improving the material conditions of individuals, the environment and community.

“A publicly owned supermarket with cheaper food is wildly popular, because it makes people’s lives better,” he told Guardian Australia.

“Of course this is the sort of policy that we should be discussing right now.”

Shoebridge said Mamdani’s message about the government needing to address the needs of citizens was working.

“When I talk to people, I hear about the dread they feel heading down the supermarket aisle, the shopping trolley feels like pushing a boulder up to the checkout,” he said.

“While 99% of us are paying more for food, and many are making decisions about enough food or some other essentials, the 1% who own Coles and Woolies are laughing.”

The competition watchdog has brought cases against both Coles and Woolworths over false or misleading representations about in-store discounts, and a report released last year found they were among the most profitable grocers in the world.

The Greens allege Labor’s new laws banning supermarkets from excessive pricing are ineffective and have not resulted in lower costs for consumers.

world.title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike
world.snippet: After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underw...
world.content:
On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.

Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.

Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.

Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.

After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.

Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.

“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.

“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”

On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.

“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”

Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.

When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”

The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.

In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.

“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”

With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.

She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.

“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

world.title: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed
world.snippet: Study of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theory Court officials and craftspeopl...
world.content:
Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls.

The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC.

Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.

Writing in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, Dr Roselyn Campbell, author of the study from Purdue University in the US, notes: “While Aha, the first ruler of the First Dynasty, seems to have only had a few subsidiary burials, his successors included hundreds of subsidiary graves around their tombs and enclosures.”

The graves of the retainers were excavated in the 1920s by the English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who believed them to be an example of human sacrifice – a view some later experts agreed with.

But there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died.

Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge.

“This question of whether or not retainer sacrifice was practised in Egypt has been debated for over a century, but this is the first study to examine the human remains from the tombs themselves,” Campbell told the Guardian.

Campbell reports that 18 of the skulls showed signs of potentially lethal trauma such as fractures and – in one case – a chopping injury to the eye.

Campbell believs Petrie may have seen the skull fractures but did not realise they were injuries that occurred around the time of death, rather than arising as a result of later damage.

The fractures, she adds, are unlikely to have been caused by a mace – a weapon often depicted in ancient Egyptian art as being used by a victorious king to smite his enemies. Instead they are more likely to have been caused by flat, wide objects made of wood or antler.

“For the crania without trauma, we cannot be certain they were sacrificed. It’s quite possible that some of the retainers were sacrificed, while others were not,” she said. “With such a small sample size of the original burial population, we simply can’t see the full extent of these funerary rituals, nor can we be sure that this sample is truly representative of all the retainers.”

Campbell noted the number of subsidiary graves tapered off quickly and seems to have disappeared with the beginning of the Second Dynasty.

Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, said while the idea of retainer sacrifice was not totally new, “this paper is one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains”.

She added: “The practice was short-lived, with people being replaced by statuettes. Possibly some or all retainers felt that this was a boon and that they would enjoy an eternal life in the service of the god-king, though they might also have resented it, been terrified, and tried to escape this fate.”

Dr Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University, Alabama, said similar sacrifices had occurred across different cultures and times, adding that not everyone at the Egyptian site may have been compliant.

“If you really think about what those scenes would have looked like, it would have been very gruesome,” she said. While noting that the study only involved a small number of skulls from the burial site, “the idea that some of the people may have been violently killed, I think, is something that in reality we might expect”, she said.

world.title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained
world.snippet: Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown An Egyptian journalist has...
world.content:
An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.

Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.

On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said.

Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.

Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”.

“My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?”

The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing.

Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday.

The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts.

More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff.

The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war.

The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human rights record, but has largely kept funds flowing.

This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total, as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, according to a state department memo revealed by Reuters.

While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.”

Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”.

Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed.

Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on the Reporters Without Borders Press freedom index. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsadaash are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.

world.title: Libyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilities
world.snippet: Western Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks down Allegations that the son of the Liby...
world.content:
Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in western Libya have upended plans for the Tripoli-based government of national unity (GNU) to continue cooperating with Haftar on a plan to unify the country.

Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so-called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been seen by the US as an important figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions.

But a round of drone attacks in August worsened electricity blackouts in the west of the country, putting intense popular pressure on the GNU led by the prime minister, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.

Libya has been split between the east, dominated by Haftar, and the west, governed by the GNU, since the fall of Col Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, leaving the oil-rich country at the mercy of corruption, militia, migrant traffickers and myriad external actors.

Donald Trump’s Africa adviser, Massad Boulos, has hatched a plan to unify the two Libyan governments in which Haftar from the east would take on the role of president and a member of the Dbeibah family from the west would become prime minister.

Boulos has insisted he is not trying a quick fix that entrenches family elites in Libya. “It’s not about families or names,” Boulos said when asked about the reported Haftar-Dbeibah deal, before adding: “At the end of the day, those are individuals that have to be in one position or the other.”

But the drone strikes, it is claimed, were prompted by Haftar’s anger at Dbeibah apparently stalling on the Boulos merger plan and by Tripoli allegedly encouraging tribes in southern Libya to attack and kill his forces.

Over more than five days in August, drones attacked the Zawiya oil station and fuel storage facilities in western Libya. The drone strikes hit the gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a large fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5m litres of fuel when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation.

On 5 September, three Libyans and one Spanish citizen were arrested in southern Tripoli by the GNU for their alleged role in a plot that was intended to include an attack on Tripoli airport. It was thought the whole group involved five Spaniards and four Libyans. The three arrested Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the Tareq ben Ziyad brigade, an LNA formation. Information that has emerged from interviews about the plot, and Saddam Haftar’s alleged role, not just in Libya, has been described as a goldmine, capable of weakening Khalifa Haftar.

Sources in the GNU said the alleged plotters were working for Saddam Haftar. “No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam,” the sources said.

The claims not only damage Saddam Haftar’s role in the Boulos plan but also the parallel UN sponsored 4+4 talks involving the main four political institutions in Libya that led to an August agreement to stage elections within two years. The deal endorsed by the UN security council overcomes previous obstacles to elections, and had been backed by the main actors capable of delivering the change.

Walid Ellafi, minister for state for political affairs in the UN-backed Libyan GNU and an enthusiast for elections, said: “Our support for the 4+4 process is rooted in its role as a UN sponsored framework offering a new approach to achieving practical results that pave the way for elections and institutions whose political legitimacy derives from the will of the people – not as a political settlement that overlooks violations or sets aside the rights of those affected.”

He opposes an elite east-west political deal that brushes aside longstanding grievances such as the displacement of 9,000 families in Benghazi during the 2014 war.

The allegations about the sabotage operation may intensify a power struggle between the three sons of Khalifa Haftar in the east.

Saddam Haftar is seen as his father’s most likely heir, possesses the most resources, enjoys the backing of the United Arab Emirates and has so far dominated the political tracks. But his brothers, Khaled and Belqasim – more allied with Egypt than the United Arab Emirates – have recently started to challenge his dominance.

world.title: Row erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skin
world.snippet: Artwork created in Tahrir Square for Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric cla...
world.content:
On the eve of the Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight.

Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by a group of young volunteers, Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square.

But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the 14th-century BCE pharaoh’s origins. The artwork vanished under fresh paint just hours before Xi landed.

Now, Ahmed Moussa, the 22-year-old founder of Rasmet Basma, has admitted it was asked by the Cairo governorate to paint over its work, which had been prepared in just five days in late August.

The team used the AI programme ChatGPT to generate the designs, which volunteers then painted on to the wall.

Moussa said Cairo’s deputy governor and the head of the district had visited the site throughout the process and were impressed by the murals – until controversy began to build on social media.

“We used a golden-bronze tone that cast a kind of shadow on the faces at night, so they appeared dark-skinned,” Moussa said.

“We acknowledge our mistake in not consulting specialists in archaeology and art.”

Afrocentrism is a political movement asserting that ancient Egyptian civilisation was black African in origin and population.

One user asked whether anyone involved had “even seen what Nefertiti actually looked like”, while others accused Afrocentric groups of appropriating the images to claim Egyptians endorsed their theories.

Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, said the volunteers should not have been allowed to paint a city site as significant as Tahrir Square without expert oversight, and that the public outrage was justified.

“Claims linking ancient Egyptian civilisation to sub-Saharan Africa are nonsense,” Hawass said.

“Temple carvings from the late period show Egyptian kings depicted alongside captives from parts of Africa, Libya, Syria and Palestine, with the king himself not shown as dark-skinned,” he said.

This is just the latest episode in a long-running debate over the complexion of ancient Egyptians. In 2023, a Netflix documentary provoked discussion after casting a dark-skinned actor as Cleopatra, and a similar dispute flared in June 2024 after a guide reportedly gave an Afrocentric perspective of Egyptian history in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.

Monica Hanna, a prominent Egyptologist and assistant professor of archaeology at the American University of Iraq–Baghdad, labelled Afrocentric claims “pseudoscience”. She said Egyptian society had always been ethnically diverse, from Nubian communities in the south to Mediterranean populations in the north.

“Egyptians were never one skin colour,” she said. “We are not snow-white, or the colour of cream.”

Walid Mahmoud, an AI researcher and expert in African anthropology, said AI tools such as ChatGPT reflected whatever information was most widely shared online, rather than what was factually accurate.

They were built by companies in the US and Europe, he said, and the content they generated could shape how those audiences saw themselves.

“That’s why we should never simply accept what it produces, especially when it comes to cultural identity and heritage,” Mahmoud said.

Mostafa Eissa, an art critic, said AI should remain a tool, never a decision-maker in its own right.

“I favour using technology without abandoning the human element within the artist,” he said, warning that letting such tools substitute an artist’s own skill risked emptying a work of its originality.

  • This article is published in collaboration with Egab
